Big picture

Why the neck is divided into triangles

The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle is the key landmark of the neck. On each side, it splits the neck into an anterior triangle (in front of the SCM) and a posterior triangle (behind the SCM) — a system that lets clinicians describe location, and predict which structures are at risk, with precision.

How the division works

A vertical midline runs down the front of the neck, splitting the body — and therefore the neck — into right and left halves. On each side, the sternocleidomastoid muscle runs obliquely from the mastoid process down to the sternum and clavicle, further subdividing that half into two regions:

  • Anterior triangle — bounded by the midline, the lower border of the mandible, and the anterior border of SCM.
  • Posterior triangle — bounded by the posterior border of SCM, the anterior border of trapezius, and the clavicle.

Every triangle can be described the same way

Throughout this lecture, each triangle (and sub-triangle) is described using the same four features — this is the framework to memorize:

Anterior triangle

Boundaries, apex, roof & floor

The anterior triangle is the region in front of the sternocleidomastoid. It is described first as a single triangle, then subdivided into four smaller triangles.

Boundaries HIGH-YIELD

SuperiorLower border (body) of the mandible
AnteriorMidline of the neck
Anterior
TriangleApex at the jugular (suprasternal) notch
PosteriorAnterior border of sternocleidomastoid
BaseDirected upward, toward the mandible

The triangle is described as "upside down": its apex points inferiorly, located at the jugular notch in the manubrium sterni, while its base lies superiorly along the mandible.

Roof & Floor

Roof

Formed by the superficial fascia, which contains the platysma muscle (a muscle of facial expression) together with subcutaneous tissue — loose connective tissue plus fat.

Floor

Formed by three midline viscera, from superior to inferior:

  • Pharynx — subdivided into nasopharynx, oropharynx (via the oropharyngeal isthmus), and laryngopharynx
  • Larynx
  • Thyroid gland — lies anterior to the thyroid and cricoid cartilages

1

Submental Triangle

Unpaired · midline of the suprahyoid region
▾

Boundaries HIGH-YIELD

  • Inferior: body of the hyoid bone
  • Lateral (×2): anterior belly of the right digastric muscle, and anterior belly of the left digastric muscle

Contents

Submental lymph nodes Small veins → anterior jugular vein

Small veins within the triangle unite to form the anterior jugular vein, which then descends in the neck.

The hyoid bone

A horseshoe-shaped bone with no bony articulation to any other bone. It has a body, two greater horns, and two lesser horns — the body lies at the junction between the greater and lesser horns on each side.

2

Digastric (Submandibular) Triangle

Paired · beneath the body of the mandible
▾

Boundaries HIGH-YIELD

  • Superior: inferior border of the mandible
  • Antero-inferior: anterior belly of the digastric muscle
  • Postero-inferior: posterior belly of the digastric muscle

Contents

Submandibular gland Submandibular lymph nodes Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) Facial artery & vein (parts) Submental artery (branch of facial a.)

Salivary glands, quick recap

Small glands sit within the mucosa/submucosa of the lips, gingiva, and hard palate. The three paired large glands are the parotid (anterior to the ear), submandibular (along the lower border of the mandible), and sublingual (beneath the tongue).

3

Carotid Triangle

Paired · the neurovascular hub of the neck
▾

Boundaries HIGH-YIELD

  • Superior: posterior belly of the digastric muscle
  • Antero-superior: superior belly of the omohyoid muscle
  • Posterior: anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid

Contents — the carotid sheath HIGH-YIELD

A tube of deep cervical fascia — the carotid sheath — contains three structures:

Common carotid artery Internal jugular vein Vagus nerve (CN X)

Also within the triangle: the carotid sinus (a baroreceptor), the carotid body (a chemoreceptor), the ansa cervicalis loop, and deep cervical lymph nodes.

Arterial branching

The common carotid artery bifurcates into external and internal carotid arteries at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. The external carotid gives off: superior thyroid, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, and ascending pharyngeal arteries.

Internal jugular vein

Begins as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus at the jugular foramen, descends through the neck, and joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein — which in turn forms the superior vena cava.

The Vagus Nerve & Deep Cervical Lymphatics

Two structures that travel the length of the carotid sheath and connect the neck to the thorax and abdomen.

Vagus nerve (CN X) course HIGH-YIELD

A mixed nerve (motor + sensory fibers) that:

  • Leaves the skull through the jugular foramen, alongside the internal jugular vein
  • Descends through the neck within the carotid sheath, lying posterior to the internal jugular vein and common carotid artery
  • Passes through the posterior mediastinum of the thorax
  • Passes behind the root of the lung (the hilar bundle of bronchus, pulmonary vessels, lymphatics and sympathetics, wrapped in pleura)
  • Enters the abdomen through the esophageal opening of the diaphragm

Abdominal distribution

Forms the esophageal and cardiac plexuses, then distributes to the liver, kidneys, spleen, and the entire small intestine, continuing into the large intestine. Its parasympathetic supply ends at the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon — beyond that point (the distal third of the transverse colon through the rectum), pelvic splanchnic (parasympathetic) nerves take over.

Its name ("vagus" = wanderer) is often explained playfully as the nerve that "wanders" the farthest of all cranial nerves — from skull base to colon.

Deep cervical lymph nodes & drainage

  • Form a vertical chain running along the course of the internal jugular vein
  • Receive lymph from all lymph nodes of the head and neck (via regional groups such as submental and submandibular nodes)
  • Their efferent vessels unite to form the jugular trunk on each side
SideJugular trunk drains into
RightRight lymphatic duct
LeftThoracic duct

Afferent vessels carry lymph into a node; efferent vessels carry lymph out of a node.

Posterior triangle

Boundaries, apex, roof & floor

The region behind the sternocleidomastoid and in front of trapezius.

Boundaries HIGH-YIELD

ApexSuperior nuchal line of the occipital bone
AnteriorPosterior border of sternocleidomastoid
Posterior
Triangle
PosteriorAnterior border of trapezius
InferiorMiddle third of the clavicle

The apex is where SCM and trapezius meet, near the external occipital protuberance, along the superior nuchal line (one of three nuchal lines on the occipital bone: supreme, superior, and inferior).

Roof & Floor

Roof

Skin, superficial fascia, and the investing layer of deep cervical fascia — the same fascial layer that roofs the anterior triangle.

Floor

Muscles covered by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia:

Splenius capitis Levator scapulae Scalenus medius (± scalenus anterior / posterior)

Nerves, Vessels & Lymph Nodes of the Posterior Triangle

Nerves HIGH-YIELD

Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) — the single most important nerve here; superficial and vulnerable to iatrogenic injury during neck surgery, especially lymph node biopsy. Also: branches of the cervical plexus, and the roots and trunks of the brachial plexus.

Vessels

Subclavian artery (3rd part) Transverse cervical artery Suprascapular artery Occipital artery (at apex) External jugular vein → subclavian vein

Lymph nodes

Supraclavicular lymph nodes.
